prompt: What does a policer do with a packet that arrives when the rate has been used up?

choices.text: Holds it in a queue until there is room
choices.why: That is a shaper, and it costs delay.

choices.text: Drops it, or re-marks it
choices.why: Right. Nothing waits; the excess is gone or demoted.

choices.text: Sends it anyway and bills the customer for it
choices.why: A policer enforces the rate; it does not meter extra use.

choices.text: Splits it into fragments small enough to fit
choices.why: Fragmenting changes size, not rate: the same bytes would still be over.

prompt: Which symptom does a shaper cause that a policer does not?

choices.text: Steady loss that TCP has to retransmit
choices.why: That is the policer's symptom: 1337 retransmissions in this lesson.

choices.text: Extra delay, as packets wait their turn
choices.why: Right. 22 ms for a ping through the shaper, 0.070 ms through the policer.

choices.text: Bursts clipped at the rate, with nothing delayed
choices.why: Clipping without delay is exactly what a policer does.

choices.text: A new DSCP value on the packets over the rate
choices.why: Re-marking is one of a policer's options, not a shaper's.

prompt: Match each term to what it does.
hint: Two limits and the mechanism they share.

pairs.right: Keeps the excess and sends it later
Discards the excess on the spot
Decides whether rate is left for a packet

prompt: How many bytes a second does a 5 Mbit/s token bucket earn?
An empty bucket of 16,384 bytes refills at 625,000 bytes a second. How many milliseconds until it is full?
What does the bucket's size, the burst, decide?
hint: Tokens saved up while the link was quiet.

choices.text: The average rate over a minute
choices.why: The rate decides that; the size only lets it be exceeded briefly.

choices.text: How much may go at once after a quiet spell
choices.why: Right. 16 KB is about ten full-size frames straight through.

choices.text: How long a packet may wait before it is dropped
choices.why: That is the shaper's queue limit, latency 50ms here.

choices.text: How many queues the link has
choices.why: A token bucket has no queues at all; classes do.

prompt: A policer is configured with a bucket of 1000 bytes. What happens to 1514-byte frames?
hint: How many tokens can the bucket ever hold?

choices.text: They pass, at a lower rate
choices.why: A frame needs 1514 tokens at once, and the bucket never holds that many.

choices.text: One passes each time the bucket refills
choices.why: A full bucket is 1000 tokens, still short of 1514.

choices.text: Not one of them ever passes
choices.why: Right. The bucket must be at least one frame deep.

choices.text: The policer fragments them to fit
choices.why: A policer passes or drops; it never rewrites a packet's size.

prompt: Given the same burst of 40 frames, the model's shaper sent all 40, and its policer sent 18 and ___ 22.
hint: It did not wait for tokens.

prompt: Through the shaper, the upload lost 248 packets in its first second and none after. Why none after?
hint: What does a shaper do with an early packet?

choices.text: TCP switches retransmission off after a loss
choices.why: TCP never switches it off; there was simply nothing to resend.

choices.text: The shaper held each packet until its tokens came
choices.why: Right. Once TCP settled at the rate, the queue absorbed the rest.

choices.text: The ISP began buffering the extra packets
choices.why: The ISP had no limit configured in this run.

choices.text: The bucket grew to fit the upload
choices.why: tc -s still shows burst 16Kb.

prompt: The shaped upload's sender line says 6.42 Mbits/sec and its receiver line 4.70. Which describes the link?
hint: One of them counts bytes still queued.

choices.text: The sender's 6.42, since it sent them
choices.why: It counts what went into its socket, including the first second's backlog.

choices.text: The average of the two, about 5.56
choices.why: Averaging a wrong figure with a right one gives a wrong one.

choices.text: The receiver's 4.70: what arrived
choices.why: Right. And 5 × 1448 ÷ 1514 caps the file at about 4.78.

choices.text: The per-second 5.24, the steadiest number
choices.why: That column is counted at the sender too, in iperf3's blocks.

prompt: A ping during the shaped upload took about 22 ms. What was it waiting for?

choices.text: The shaper holds ICMP back on purpose
choices.why: tbf does not know what a ping is; it has one queue for everything.

choices.text: A full 16 KB bucket before each ping
choices.why: A ping needs 98 tokens, not a full bucket.

choices.text: About 14 KB of the upload ahead of it in the queue
choices.why: Right. 14.1 KB at 5 Mbit/s is about 23 ms.

choices.text: The ISP's router, which slows under load
choices.why: Under the policer, with the same upload, the ping took 0.070 ms.

prompt: A shaper at 4.5 Mbit/s counts 1514-byte frames, each carrying 1448 bytes of the file. What is the most the file can reach, in Mbit/s?
Under the policer, a ping took 0.070 ms while the upload ran. Why so fast?

choices.text: A policer has no queue to wait in
choices.why: Right. A packet fits the bucket and goes, or does not and is dropped.

choices.text: The policer gives ICMP priority
choices.why: The rule matches every packet from 203.0.113.2, pings included.

choices.text: The upload had already finished
choices.why: It started two seconds into the eight-second upload.

choices.text: The ISP's router is faster than hq
choices.why: Both are namespaces on the same computer.

prompt: The policer counted 1335 packets and 2,002,500 bytes. What does dividing one by the other say?

choices.text: That most of the dropped packets were pings
choices.why: A ping is 84 bytes; these average exactly 1500.

choices.text: That every dropped packet was a full 1500-byte one
choices.why: Right. The drops fell on the upload's full-size segments.

choices.text: That the drops were spread over every size
choices.why: An exact 1500 average from 1335 packets leaves no room for small ones.

choices.text: That the policer drops headers and keeps data
choices.why: A policer drops whole packets or none.

prompt: A voice call shares the policed link with a large upload. What does the call suffer?

choices.text: Delay, as its packets queue behind the upload
choices.why: There is no queue to stand in; that was the shaper.

choices.text: Gaps, when its packets meet an empty bucket
choices.why: Right. They are dropped, not delayed, and voice has no time to resend.

choices.text: Nothing, since a policer drops only TCP
choices.why: The rule matches by address, whatever the protocol.

choices.text: Echo, from voice packets that are sent twice
choices.why: Voice over UDP does not retransmit; a lost packet stays lost.

prompt: Under the policer, the Cwnd column swung between 5.66 and 129 KBytes. Why?

choices.text: The policer resizes TCP's window directly
choices.why: A policer only drops; the sender changes its own window.

choices.text: iperf3 changes its block size every second
choices.why: The blocks stay the same; the per-second column reads 640 KBytes throughout.

choices.text: TCP grows until a run is dropped, then cuts back
choices.why: Right. With no queue to absorb a burst, every climb ends in a loss.

choices.text: The receiver's buffer keeps filling and emptying
choices.why: Cwnd is the sender's congestion window, not the receiver's buffer.

prompt: With hq shaping at 4500 kbit, the policer's counter stayed at 0 packets. Where were the 208 retransmitted packets lost?
hint: The only other limit on the path.

choices.text: At the ISP's policer, which counts only some drops
choices.why: The counter counts every packet the rule drops.

choices.text: At web1, which could not keep up
choices.why: web1 took 2.91 Gbit/s at the start of the lesson.

choices.text: At hq's own shaper
choices.why: Right. Inside the customer's router, in a queue the customer controls.

choices.text: Nowhere: iperf3 counts duplicates as retransmissions
choices.why: A retransmission is a segment sent again because the first was lost.

prompt: Why is the customer's shaper set a little below the contracted rate rather than exactly at it?

choices.text: Providers charge extra at exactly the contracted rate
choices.why: The rate is what was bought; nothing extra is charged for using it.

choices.text: They count bytes differently, and need room for it
choices.why: Right. Frame or packet, their own bucket and clock: the margin absorbs the difference.

choices.text: A shaper set at the rate would drop every packet
choices.why: The 5 Mbit/s shaper delivered 4.70 Mbit/s with no losses after the first second.

choices.text: The policer lets nothing through above 90% of the rate
choices.why: It passed 5.37 Mbit/s on its own; there is no 90% rule in it.

prompt: What does the customer gain by shaping just under the contract? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The losses happen in its own router
choices.why: Right: the policer counted 0.

choices.text: More throughput than the policer alone allowed
choices.why: It got less: 4.31 Mbit/s against 5.37.

choices.text: A queue its QoS classes can arrange
choices.why: Right: the bottleneck is now in its router, where lesson 18's classes act.

choices.text: No queueing delay at all
choices.why: A shaper is a queue; the delay moves to your router, it does not vanish.

prompt: Put in order what a shaper does with one full-size frame when its bucket is short.
hint: It never drops a frame that fits its queue.
items: The frame arrives and joins the queue
The bucket is topped up for the time since it was last checked
The frame waits until the bucket holds 1514 tokens
The frame leaves, and its 1514 tokens are removed
trap: A policer would stop at the third step and drop the frame instead of waiting.

prompt: A small office's calls break up during uploads. Its 20 Mbit/s line is policed by the provider. What should the office configure?
hint: Own the bottleneck, then arrange it.

choices.text: A policer at 20 Mbit/s on its own router
choices.why: A second policer adds loss and gives the calls no queue to be put first in.

choices.text: A shaper a little under 20 Mbit/s, with a voice class inside it
choices.why: Right. The queue forms in the office's router, and the voice class skips it.

choices.text: Nothing, since the provider's policer already limits the rate
choices.why: It limits it by dropping, calls included, with no way to prefer them.

choices.text: A shaper above 20 Mbit/s, to use every bit bought
choices.why: Above the contract, the provider's policer drops the excess and the shaper never forms a queue.

prompt: Match each counter from this lesson to where it was counted.

pairs.right: The policer on the ISP's router
